newsitem.title: USA: Chateau, ROC deal raises REIT issue.
newsitem.headline: Chateau, ROC deal raises REIT issue.

text.p: Chateau Properties Inc's decision to revise a merger proposal with ROC Communities and turn down acquisition offers has created concern over who rules a real estate investment trust (REIT), analysts said Wednesday.
"Primarily the whole focus came down to the treatment of the OP (operating partnership) unit holders versus the shareholders," said Kevin Comer, an analyst for BT Securities.
Chateau has shareholders, who vote and elect a board of directors, and OP unit holders, who do not vote and are mostly the REIT's directors and managers.

Early Wednesday, Chateau and ROC said they had revised a merger agreement, giving Chateau shareholders 1.0316 shares of the merged company for each Chateau share. The previous agreement provided a one-for-one exchange.

Also included in the new deal was an option for OP unit holders to swap units for common shares. Using the tax code 351, the unit holders defer what would be significant capital gains taxes. There are more units than Chateau shares.
Chateau advised against a $26 a share cash tender offer by Manufactured Home Communities Inc, a firm run by Sam Zell, adding the company is not for sale.
Chateau and ROC maintain that their "merger of equals" agreement reached in July would benefit common shareholders.
"It is a long-term strategic business combination that we are convinced is going to be in the long-term interest of shareholders," ROC chief executive Gary McDaniel said.
He and Chateau chief executive Jeff Kellogg said in an interview the companies' properties and management teams merge well, and the executives expect growth in the new company.
In addition, the unit holders who accept the transfer to shares would waive rights to a 3.16 percent stock dividend, which Chateau said would be given to the shareholders.

Nonetheless, the analysts said the MHC offer of $26 is hard to beat for shareholders but is not attractive for OP unit holders because of tax reasons. Chateau turned down Sun Communities Inc's offer for a merger as well.
"I don't think for the shareholder there is $26 of value in the merger," said Jim Sullivan, an analyst for Green Street Advisors.

According to Fred Jacobs, director of the Master of Business Taxation program at the University of Minnesota, code 351 can be used only if after the transfer the unit holders own 80 percent of the company's common shares.

"The key is they receive control," Jacobs said. "Here they are not entirely losing their interest -- they are changing the form of their ownership and are therefore allowed to defer the recognition of their gain.... What it does is fully utilize the rules available to them," Jacobs said.

There are 6.1 million Chateau common shares outstanding, and the company said certain OP unit holders intend to convert another six million. Chateau said it would buy up to 1.45 million shares and ROC would buy about 350,000.
Kellogg and McDaniel said they hope to close the deal by the end of 1996. Next, ROC shareholders must vote on the deal.
While Chateau advised against MHC's offer, it is still available. "We are just getting the details," MHC's Zell said. "But I would highly doubt it puts an end to our offer."

Analysts said they expect the debate over the REIT's OP unit holders and shareholders to continue. "I don't think I ever imagined they would create a structure where OP unit holders would be able to transfer tax-free. It's unprecedented and creates concern in the REIT industry," Comer said.
